segments.text: There's no safe handling of dangerous or flammable materials without effective storage.
That's when the materials are going to spend most of their time, and adequate handling
is essential.
Storing flammable liquids, for example, will have to be done with an approved flammable
storage cabinet, including safety labels like flammable keep fire away.
The containers themselves have to be approved and rated for each material.
According to OSHA, only approved containers and portable tanks shall be used for storage
and handling of flammable liquids.
Approved safety cans or Department of Transportation approved containers shall be used for the handling
and use of flammable liquids in quantities of five gallons or less, except that this
shall not apply to those flammable liquid materials which are highly-visit, extremely
hard to pour, which may be used and handled in original shipping containers.
For quantities of one gallon or less, the original container may be used for storage,
use and handling of flammable liquids.
Adhering to OSHA's guidelines might seem a little overly restrictive, but the key here
is that every employee should have full knowledge of a container's contents before working
with it.
If you don't communicate what's inside a container, it incurs all sorts of additional
risks and potential liabilities.
As Berkeley notes, keep explosive chemicals away from ignition sources such as open
flames, hot surfaces, spark sources, and direct sunlight, and consider designating
a special area for explosive chemical use.
How about we break that down in some further detail?
What does proper storage look like beyond the container?
Want some key points to remember?
First, flammable liquids can't be stored in areas used for exits, stairways, or other
high-traffic areas.
No more than 25 gallons of flammable liquids can be stored in a room outside of an approved
storage cabinet.
Quantities of flammable liquid exceeding 25 gallons have to be stored in a cabinet that
meets OSHA requirement.
And finally, any materials which may react with water to create a fire hazard should
not be stored in the same room with flammable liquid.
According to OSHA, all relevant personnel should have immediate and easy access to safety
data sheets.
This will be a detailed document outlining important hazardous information related to specific materials.
After all, each chemical has unique properties, and no one should handle or store the chemical
until the full workplace safety rules are planned and trained on.
Proper training, of course, is a topic all its own, and you'll find that there are no
universal OSHA-accepted certification courses for specific hazardous materials.
What you should expect is guidance on how to conduct training for your workspace that
helps you meet OSHA standards and keep your employees in the know.
